No, a local override plus a code comment isn't enough — you've fixed your own exposure but the other three teams are still shipping the same leak with zero awareness of it. A few things to do:

1. **Notify the other three teams directly** (sales, onboarding, internal-tools bot owners) — don't rely on them stumbling onto your comment or a changelog. Send each a concrete notice: what the bug is (prompt-truncation edge case causing internal tool/DB identifiers to leak into customer-facing output), how to reproduce it, severity, and your fix as a workaround they can adopt immediately.

2. **Fix it upstream in `prompt-common`**, not just in your local override. A local patch that quietly diverges from the shared package is itself a latent bug — someone will "helpfully" resync your bot to the shared template later and reintroduce the leak. Push the fix as a PR/change to the package (or file it with whoever owns that package) so all four consumers get the real fix, not four different local patches.

3. **Treat this as a security-relevant disclosure, not just a formatting bug.** Leaking internal database query tool identifiers to customers is information disclosure — it could help an attacker map your internal tooling/attack surface. That bumps the urgency: this should go through whatever incident/security reporting channel you have, not just an informal heads-up.

4. **Record it as a shared-defect report** tied to your OPEX record and deficiency register (per your process) — description, severity, affected consumers, fix/workaround, and an owner for each notification. This creates a paper trail so it doesn't silently die if people are slow to act on a Slack message.

Since I don't have access to your actual `prompt-common` package, team contacts, or tracker in this environment, I can't send those notices or file the report for you — but if you want, I can help you draft the incident write-up / notification message and the PR description for the upstream fix.
